title: The summit kettle
hook: Water boils at 100 °C. Does it on top of Everest?

knows: that water boils at 100 °C at sea level
that air is thinner high up
doesNotKnow: that the boiling point depends on the air pressure on the water

objective: The learner can explain that water boils when its vapour pressure equals the air pressure, so at about 0.31 atm on Everest's summit it boils at about 69 °C.

claims.text: Air pressure on the summit of Mount Everest is about 0.3 atm (sea level: 1 atm).
claims.source: ICAO standard atmosphere at 8,850 m: p/p0 = (1 - 2.25577e-5 x 8850)^5.25588 = 0.310 (node, Demo.tsx air()). Measured summit pressures are about 31 to 34 kPa, i.e. 0.31 to 0.34 atm (West 1983/1999: 253 mmHg = 33.7 kPa = 0.333 atm), higher than the standard atmosphere because of the warm tropical air column. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Standard-atmosphere value 0.310 reproduced. Measured summit pressure is 253 mmHg = 33.7 kPa = 0.333 atm (West 1983/1999); the cited West 2006 HAMB 7(2) paper was not located. "About 0.31" holds loosely; recommend "about 0.3 atm". | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Wording per checker: 'about 0.3 atm' (standard atmosphere gives 0.310; measured summit 253 mmHg = 0.333 atm, West 1983/1999). Predict question and reveal now say 0.3. The West 2006 HAMB 7(2) citation could not be located and is replaced by West 1983/1999.

claims.text: Water on the summit of Everest boils at about 70 °C.
claims.source: Clausius-Clapeyron with dH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol held constant and 1 atm at 373.15 K: 1/T = 1/373.15 + (8.314/40700) ln(1/0.310); T = 342.6 K = 69.4 °C (node). Published summit boiling points are about 68 to 71 °C. At the measured 0.33 atm the model gives about 71 °C. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Model 69.4 C at 0.31 atm; 71 C at the measured 0.33 atm. "About 69" is within the published 68-71 range. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Wording per checker: 'about 70 C' (model 69.4 C at 0.31 atm, 71 C at measured 0.33 atm, published 68 to 71). Predict option and reveal now say 70 (B_SAY rounds the model to the nearest 5; the stage readout still shows the model's own value).

claims.text: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure of the air on it; at sea level (1 atm) that is at 100 °C.
claims.source: Definition of boiling point (IUPAC Gold Book; Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, ch. 4). Normal boiling point of water 99.97 °C at 101.325 kPa (CRC Handbook).

claims.text: The curve is water's vapour pressure from a model with a constant heat of vaporisation (40.7 kJ/mol) and the air line comes from the standard atmosphere.
claims.source: dH_vap of water 40.65 kJ/mol at 100 °C (CRC Handbook). The constant-dH Clausius-Clapeyron curve overestimates vapour pressure at room temperature (0.031 vs 0.026 atm at 22 °C) but is within about 1 °C of steam tables for the boiling point between 0.3 and 1 atm. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Reproduced: model 0.0312 atm at 22 C vs 0.0261 true.

claims.text: Food in water boiling at a lower temperature cooks more slowly.
claims.source: Cooking rates rise steeply with temperature (Arrhenius); high-altitude cooking guidance (USDA, 'High Altitude Cooking') advises longer cooking times.

claims.text: (Recall) Water under 2 atm boils at about 120 °C.
claims.source: Steam tables: saturation temperature 120.2 °C at 202.6 kPa (CRC Handbook / IAPWS-IF97). The lesson's constant-dH model gives 120.8 °C (node). · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Model gives 120.8 C; steam table 120.2 C.

recall.question: A pressure cooker raises the pressure on the water above 1 atm. The water inside boils…
recall.why: Water boils when its vapour pressure matches the pressure on it; more pressure needs hotter water (about 120 °C at 2 atm).
